nodes.name: Minimal in looking down
nodes.statement:
A space $X$ is \emph{mimimal} in looking down if every space
$Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$.
differentia: every space $Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$

nodes.name: BPI equivalence implies look-down equivalence
nodes.statement:
BPI equivalence of spaces $X$ and $Y$ implies that $X$ and $Y$ are
\emph{look-down equivalent}, meaning that $X$ looks down on $Y$ and $Y$ looks down on $X$.

nodes.name: Laakso: look-down equivalence does not imply BPI equivalence
nodes.statement: However, Laakso has shown that the converse is not true in general \cite{laakso-bpi}.

nodes.name: Kirchheim: Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down
nodes.statement:
For example, from the result of
Kirchheim \cite{Kirchheim} we know that Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down.

nodes.name: Quantitative Kirchheim theorem (Schul)
David-Semmes Problem 11.15 (minimality of the Heisenberg group in looking down)
nodes.statement:
David and Semmes asked in Problem 11.15 of \cite{davsem} if the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is also minimal 
in looking down, when equipped with sub-Riemannian distances, also called  Carnot-Carath\'eodory distances.
nodes.origin_citation: David & Semmes, Problem 11.15; Heinonen & Semmes, Question 22
nodes.statement_short: Is the sub-Riemannian Heisenberg group minimal in looking down?

nodes.name: Non-minimality of the Heisenberg group in looking down
nodes.statement: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down.
conclusions: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down.
nodes.label: thm:Hnotminimal

nodes.name: Countably n-rectifiable metric measure space
nodes.statement:
Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is countably $n$-rectifiable if there exist a countable set of
Borel subsets $A_i \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and Lipschitz maps $f : A_i \to X$ 
such that $\mu\left(X \backslash \bigcup_i f(A_i) \right) = 0$ and $\mu \ll \mathcal H^n$ where $\mathcal H^n$ is the Hausdorff $n$-measure.
nodes.statement_short: Countably many Lipschitz images of Borel subsets of R^n cover X up to measure zero, and mu << H^n.

nodes.name: Kirchheim: rectifiable pieces can be taken biLipschitz
nodes.statement:
It was shown in \cite{Kirchheim} that, by further countably decomposing each $f(A_i)$ if necessary, 
one may assume that each $f_i$ is biLipschitz.

nodes.name: H-rectifiability
nodes.statement:
One can easily create a definition of being $\mathbb H$-rectifiable by letting each $A_i$
be a Borel subset of the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ and setting $n = 4$, the Hausdorff dimension of $\mathbb H$.

nodes.name: Lipschitz image of H that is not biLipschitz rectifiable
nodes.statement:
However, we now see that there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 
4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union
of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$.
conclusions:
there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 
4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union
of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$

nodes.name: Lipschitz rectifiability is strictly weaker than biLipschitz rectifiability in Heisenberg geometry
nodes.statement: Thus, ``Lipschitz rectifiability'' is strictly weaker than ``biLipschitz rectifiability'' when using the Heisenberg geometry.

nodes.name: Ahlfors 4-regular distance on H with no biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group. There exists a distance $d$ on $\mathbb H $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq d_{cc}$; \item $(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular; \item if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: There is a distance d <= d_cc on H, Ahlfors 4-regular, biLipschitz to d_cc on no set of positive measure.
assumptions: $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group
conclusions: $d\leq d_{cc}$;
$(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular;
if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.label: thm:Heisenbergdistance

nodes.name: Lipschitz maps from H to Carnot groups have biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement:
Indeed, one can then use a similar argument as in \cite{Kirchheim},
with inspiration from \cite{pauls},
 to show that Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to another Carnot group with positive 4-measure image have biLipschitz pieces.

nodes.name: G.C. David: biLipschitz pieces for Lipschitz maps between regular LLC manifolds
nodes.statement:
Another situation where Lipschitz maps have biLipschitz pieces is when the spaces are
Ahlfors regular, linearly locally contractible topological manifolds and the target has manifold weak tangents,
see the work of G.C. David \cite{gcdavid} (this David is not the same David of David-Semmes).

nodes.name: The space (H,d) has no manifold tangents and is not LLC
nodes.statement:
We note that in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} the constructed space $(\mathbb H, d)$ neither has manifold tangents nor is linearly locally
contractible.

nodes.name: General shortcut theorem: Ahlfors-regular distance without biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and $Q>0$. Assume \begin{enumerate} \item $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$ and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r). \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Then there exists a distance $d$ on $X $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq \rho$; \item $(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: If (X,rho) is Ahlfors Q-regular and admits separated shortcuts at every scale, there is d <= rho, Ahlfors Q-regular, biLipschitz to rho on no positive-measure set.
assumptions: there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$ and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r). \end{equation}
conclusions: $d\leq \rho$;
$(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular;
if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.label: thm:general

nodes.name: Shortcut condition (1.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r).
nodes.label: e:general-metric-assumption

nodes.name: Left-translation biLipschitz distances below d_cc are locally biLipschitz to d_cc
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be a distance on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ such that $d \le d_{cc}$ and $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$. Assume that the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$. Then $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.
assumptions: $d$ be a distance on the Heisenberg group
the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$
conclusions: $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.
nodes.label: thm:positiveinvarianttobilip

nodes.name: Necessity of the assumptions of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement:
We remark that the assumptions in Theorem~\ref{thm:positiveinvarianttobilip} are necessary.
Indeed, if we don't assume  $d \le d_{cc}$, then as a counterexample
one can take two sub-Riemannian distances on $\mathbb H$ that have two different  horizontal bundles.
If we don't assume  
$\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$, then a counterexample is given by every Riemannian left-invariant distance.
Moreover, the distance $\min\{1, d_{cc}\}$ shows that the conclusion of the theorem may not be global.
nodes.statement_short: Counterexamples: different horizontal bundles, Riemannian left-invariant distances, and min{1,d_cc} (non-global).

nodes.name: Kirchheim's metric differentiation theorem
nodes.statement:
Kirchheim's result in 
 \cite{Kirchheim}
can be stated as the fact that 
every semi-distance $d$ in $\mathbb R^n$ that is smaller than the Euclidean distance
is metrically differentiable, i.e., 
 at almost every point its blow-up is a homogeneous semi-distance.

nodes.name: Pauls: horizontal metric differentiability on Carnot groups
nodes.statement:
Similarly, by \cite{Pauls01}, 
we know  that on Carnot groups semi-distances  smaller than $ d_{cc}$ 
 are metrically differentiable

   but only in the horizontal directions.

nodes.name: Kirchheim-Magnani counterexample to metric differentiability
nodes.statement:
Regarding non-horizontal directions,  from \cite{Kirchheim_Magnani} 

we know that there is
a distance 

 in the Heisenberg group that is
a counterexample to metric differentiability, although it is not biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$.

nodes.name: Self-similar (semi-)distance
nodes.statement:
If $\{\delta_\lambda\}_{\lambda>0}$ denotes the standard one-paramenter family of isomorphisms of 
$\mathbb H $, see Section \ref{sec:Heis},
a
(semi-)distance $d$ is {\em self-similar}

 if there exists 
some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $.
differentia: there exists some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $

nodes.name: Blow-up of a distance
nodes.statement:
In the following result, by {\em a blow-up} of a distance $d$
we mean any pointwise limit of the functions 
\[(p_1,p_2)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d( q_j \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_1), q_j  \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_2)) ,\]
as 
$\lambda_j \to 0$ and $q_j\in \mathbb H $.

nodes.name: Failure of Kirchheim-metric differentiation for biLipschitz maps
nodes.statement: There exist two distances $d_1, d_2$ on $\mathbb H $ that are biLipschitz equivalent to $d_{cc}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar. \item No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar.
No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar.
nodes.label: thm:fail

nodes.name: Hausdorff Q-measure
nodes.statement:
Let $Q > 0$.  Then for $A \subseteq X$, one defines
\[
 \mathcal H^Q_d(A) := \lim_{s \to 0^+} \inf \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^\infty (\operatorname{diam} E_i)^Q : A \subseteq \bigcup_i E_i \text{ an open cover}, \operatorname{diam}(E_i) < s\right\}.
\]


 We say that $\mathcal H^Q$ is the Hausdorff $Q$-measure of $(X,d)$.

nodes.name: Hausdorff measure is Borel regular
nodes.statement: It is known that the Hausdorff $Q$-measure is Borel regular although it may not be locally finite.

nodes.name: Ahlfors Q-regular metric measure space
nodes.statement:
Let $Q > 0$.  Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is said to be Ahlfors $Q$-regular if there exists $C \geq 1$ so that
  \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\operatorname{diam} X}{2}.\]
differentia:
there exists $C \geq 1$ so that
  \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\operatorname{diam} X}{2}.\]

nodes.name: Ahlfors regularity passes to Hausdorff measure
nodes.statement:
We remark that if $(X,d,\mu)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular, then 
 $(X,d,\mathcal H^Q)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular.
conclusions: $(X,d,\mathcal H^Q)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular

nodes.name: C-conformally biLipschitz map (quasi-similarity)
nodes.statement:
A biLipschitz map $f$ between metric spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ is said to be
$C$-{\em conformally biLipschitz} with scale factor $\lambda > 0$ if $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between
the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$.
differentia: $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$

nodes.name: BPI space
nodes.statement: An Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space $(X,d)$ is said to be a \emph{BPI} (``big pieces of itself'') {\em space} if there exist constants $C \ge 1$ and $\theta > 0$ such that for all $x_1,x_2 \in X$ and $0 < r_1 , r_2 < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there is a closed set $A \subseteq B(x_1,r_1)$ with $\mathcal{H}^Q(A) \ge \theta r_1^Q$ and if there is a $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x_2,r_2)$ with scale factor $r_2/r_1$.
nodes.label: def:BPI

nodes.name: BPI equivalence
nodes.statement: Two BPI spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ of the same dimension $Q$ are called \emph{BPI equivalent} if there exist constants $\theta>0$ and $C>0$ such that for each $x \in X$, $x' \in X'$ and radii $0 < R < \operatorname{diam}(X)$, $0 < R' < \operatorname{diam}(X')$ there exist a subset $A \subset B(x,R) \subset X$ with $\mathcal H^Q_d(A)\ge \theta R^Q$ and an $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x',R')$ with scale factor $R'/R$.

nodes.name: Looking down / look-down equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ be BPI metric spaces of Hausdorff dimension $Q$. The space $(X,d)$ is said to \emph{look down on} $(X',d')$ if there is a closed set $A \subset X$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon A \to X'$ such that $f(A)$ has positive Hausdorff $Q$-measure. If also $X'$ looks down on $X$, then $X$ and $X'$ are called \emph{look-down equivalent}.

nodes.statement: The Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is the simply connected Lie group whose Lie algebra is generated by three vectors $X,Y,Z$ with only non-zero relation $[X,Y]=Z$.

nodes.name: Proof of the triangle inequality for the box distance
nodes.statement:
To check that it satisfies the triangle inequality we need to show that 

 \[
 \norm{p\cdot q} \leq  \norm{p} + \norm{q}. 
 \] 
 First,
 \[  |x_{p\cdot q}|
=
|x_p +x_q|
\leq 
 |x_p| +|x_q|
 \leq 
 \norm{p} + \norm{q},
 \]
 and analogously for the $y$ component.
 Second,
  \begin{eqnarray*}
 \sqrt{   |z_{p\cdot q}|}
&=&
\sqrt{\left|z_p +z_q +\dfrac{1}{2} (x_p y_q - x_q y_p) \right|}\\
&\leq &
\sqrt{|z_p| +|z_q| +|x_p| |y_q| + |x_q| | y_p |}
\\&\leq& 
\sqrt{  \norm{p}^2 + \norm{q}^2 +2  \norm{p}  \norm{q} } 
\\& \leq &
 \norm{p} + \norm{q}.
 \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Jacobian of a homomorphism
nodes.statement:
Given a homomorphism $L : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$, one can define the Jacobian to be
 \[
   J(L) = \frac{\mathcal H^4_{d_b}(L(B_{d_b}(0,1)))}{\mathcal H_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,1))}.
 \]

nodes.name: Pansu differentiability theorem
nodes.statement:
Let $f : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to ({\mathbb H},d_b)$ be a Lipschitz map.  Pansu proved in \cite{Pansu} that for almost every $x \in {\mathbb H}$ there exists a Lipschitz homomorphism $Df(x) : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$ (the Pansu-derivative of $f$ at $x$) so that
 \[
   Df(x) (g) = \lim_{\lambda \to 0} \delta_{1/\lambda} (f(x)^{-1} f(x \delta_\lambda(g))).
 \]

conclusions: \int_{\mathbb H} N(f,A,y) d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(y) = \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x).
nodes.label: e:area-formula

nodes.name: Cost function
nodes.statement: Given a metric space $(X,\rho)$, a symmetric function $c:X\times X \to [0,\infty)$ such that $c\leq \rho$ will be called a {\em cost function}.

nodes.name: Set of shortcut pairs S
nodes.statement:
We denote by ${\mathcal S}$ all those pairs of points $(x,y)\in X\times X$ such that $c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)$
$${\mathcal S}:=\{ (x,y)\in X\times X\;:\; c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)\}.$$

nodes.name: Shortcut
nodes.statement:
An element in ${\mathcal S}$ will be called
 {\em shortcut} (or flight or tunnel).

nodes.name: Itinerary
nodes.statement:
If we have $N\in \mathbb N$ and $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ then the $N$-tuple  ${\bf x} = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N)$
will be called an {\em itinerary} from the extreme points $x_0$ to $x_N$ and we set ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x}):=(x_0,x_N)$
and $\ell({\bf x}) := N$.

nodes.name: Collection of itineraries I
nodes.statement:
We will denote by ${\mathcal I}$ the collection of all itineraries in $X$, i.e.,
$${\mathcal I}:=\{(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \;:\; N\in \mathbb N, \,x_j\in X   \}.$$

nodes.name: Cost of an itinerary
nodes.statement:
The {\em cost} of an itinerary ${\bf x}= (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}$ is
$$c ({\bf x}):= \sum_{i=1}^N c(x_{i-1}, x_i).$$

nodes.name: Distance associated to a cost function
Shortened distance d (2.5)
nodes.statement: d(x,y): = \inf\{ c ({\bf x}) \;:\; {\bf x} \in {\mathcal I} ,\, {\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(x,y)\}.
nodes.label: eq:ddef

nodes.name: d is a semi-distance, and a distance if dominated from below
nodes.statement: It is not too hard to verify symmetry and the triangle inequality for $d$ and so $d$ is a semi-distance on $X$. If there is another distance $d'$ on $X$ such that \[ d'(x,y) \leq c(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] then by the triangle inequality for $d'$, we also have that \[ d'(x,y) \leq d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] and so $d$ is then a distance.
nodes.statement_short: d satisfies symmetry and triangle inequality; if some distance d' <= c then d' <= d and d is a distance.
nodes.label: r:d'-leq-c

nodes.name: Alternating itineraries
nodes.statement:
We define the subset of {\it alternating itineraries} as
$${\mathcal I}_A:=\{{\bf x} \in {\mathcal I} \;:\;  (x_{j-1},x_{j})\in {\mathcal S} \iff j \text{ even}    \}.$$

nodes.name: Level of a shortcut / level function
nodes.statement:
We shall assign to each shortcut a natural number that we call {\em level} of the shortcut.
Namely, a function $L \colon {\mathcal S} \to \mathbb N$ will be called  a {\em level function}.

nodes.name: Level function of an alternating itinerary
Decreasing-increasing function
nodes.statement: We say that a function $f : \{1,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb R$ is {\em decreasing-increasing} if there is some $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ for which $f|_{[1,k]}$ is decreasing and $f|_{[k+1,n]}$ is increasing (both not necessarily strictly monotonically).

nodes.name: Itineraries with decreasing-increasing level function
nodes.statement:
We can then define a further subset of itineraries with decreasing-increasing level functions:
$${\mathcal I}^*:=\{{\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A \;:\;  L_{\bf x} \text{ is decreasing-increasing}    \}.$$

nodes.name: Cost ratios alpha_n
nodes.statement:
Let $(\alpha_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of real numbers in $(0,1)$ such that $\alpha_n \downarrow 0$. 
The number $\alpha_n$ will be the ratio of the cost of the level $n$ shortcut compared to the original distance of the shortcut.

nodes.name: Covering constant c_E
nodes.statement: We set $c_E \ge 4$ to be a constant that we now fix.

nodes.name: Net N_n of shortcut centres
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{N}_n := \{x_i\}$ be a set of points in
\[
 X \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_j} B_\rho(\{x,y\},
4\lambda^n)
\]
such that $\rho(x_i,x_j) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and $X \subseteq \bigcup_i B_\rho(x_i,c_E \lambda^n)$.

nodes.name: Shortcut endpoints q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}
nodes.statement:
Using assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} we select for each $i$ points $q_{i,1}, q_{i,2} \in B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n)$ such that
\[
\rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} 
\]
 and
 \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n).
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Shortcut condition at level n (3.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n).
nodes.label: e:general-metric-assumption2

nodes.name: Level n shortcuts, their costs and levels
nodes.statement:
Now define the level $n$ shortcuts as
\[
 {\mathcal S}_n := \{(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2})\,:\, i\} \cup \{(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1})\,:\, i\},
\]
their corresponding costs as
\[
 c(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := c(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := \alpha_n\rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2})
\]
and their level as
 \[
L(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) :=  L(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := n.
\]

nodes.name: All shortcuts S and the new distance d
nodes.statement:
Finally, let
\[
 {\mathcal S} := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty {\mathcal S}_n
\]
and define $d$ as in \eqref{eq:ddef}.

nodes.name: Existence of the nets N_n
nodes.statement: There exists some $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/4)$ depending only on the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$ such that if we set $\lambda \leq \lambda_0$ and $c_E = 8 + \frac1\lambda$, then we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$.
conclusions: we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$.
nodes.label: lma:constantsexist

nodes.name: Small lambda measure condition (3.2)
nodes.statement: \mu(B_\rho(x,r/4)) - \mu(B_\rho(y,\lambda r)) - \mu(B_\rho(z, \lambda r)) > 0, \qquad \forall x,y,z \in X, 0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X).
nodes.label: e:small-lambda

nodes.name: Spread of earlier shortcut points (3.3)
nodes.statement: \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}.
nodes.label: e:A-spread-out

nodes.name: Fix an Ahlfors regular measure and choose lambda small
nodes.statement_short: Fix an Ahlfors regular measure and choose lambda small

nodes.name: Introduce the set A of earlier shortcut endpoints
nodes.statement:
Let $A = \bigcup_{j < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_j} \{x,y\}$.  






  
 By the definition of $A$, each $x \in A$ comes with a pair $x' \in A$ such that $(x,x') \in S_l$ for some $l < n$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the set A of earlier shortcut endpoints

nodes.name: Claim: points of A are 2 lambda^{n-1} separated
nodes.statement:
We claim that 
 \begin{equation}
   \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}. \end{equation}
 To see this, taking $y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}$, there exists $y' \in A$ such that $(y,y') \in S_k$ for some $k < n$.
 Let $x_i^l \in \mathcal{N}_l$ such that $x,x' \in B_\rho(x_i^l,\lambda^l)$ and $x_j^k \in \mathcal{N}_k$ such that 
 $y,y' \in B_\rho(x_j^k,\lambda^k)$.
We consider two cases. Suppose  first that $k = l$. By the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$ we then have
 \[
  \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,x_j^k) - \rho(x,x_i^l) - \rho(y,x_j^k) \ge 4\lambda^k - \lambda^k - \lambda^k = 2\lambda^k \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}.
 \]
 Suppose now that $k \ne l$. By symmetry we may assume $k < l$. Then by construction, $x_i^l \notin B_\rho(y,4\lambda^l)$ and
  thus
 \[
  \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,y) - \rho(x,x_i^l) \ge 
  4\lambda^l - \lambda^l = 3\lambda^l 
  \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}.
 \]
 Thus \eqref{e:A-spread-out} is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: points of A are 2 lambda^{n-1} separated

nodes.name: Introduce centres of the two shortcuts
nodes.statement:
To see this, taking $y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}$, there exists $y' \in A$ such that $(y,y') \in S_k$ for some $k < n$.
 Let $x_i^l \in \mathcal{N}_l$ such that $x,x' \in B_\rho(x_i^l,\lambda^l)$ and $x_j^k \in \mathcal{N}_k$ such that 
 $y,y' \in B_\rho(x_j^k,\lambda^k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce centres of the two shortcuts

nodes.name: Case k = l: use separation of N_k
nodes.statement:
We consider two cases. Suppose  first that $k = l$. By the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$ we then have
 \[
  \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,x_j^k) - \rho(x,x_i^l) - \rho(y,x_j^k) \ge 4\lambda^k - \lambda^k - \lambda^k = 2\lambda^k \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}.
 \]
nodes.statement_short: Case k = l: use separation of N_k

nodes.name: Case k != l: use construction
nodes.statement:
Suppose now that $k \ne l$. By symmetry we may assume $k < l$. Then by construction, $x_i^l \notin B_\rho(y,4\lambda^l)$ and
  thus
 \[
  \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,y) - \rho(x,x_i^l) \ge 
  4\lambda^l - \lambda^l = 3\lambda^l 
  \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}.
 \]
nodes.statement_short: Case k != l: use construction

nodes.name: Separation proven
nodes.statement: Thus \eqref{e:A-spread-out} is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Separation proven

nodes.name: Take a maximal separated net outside B(A,4 lambda^n)
nodes.statement:
Let $\{x_i\}$ be a maximal $4\lambda^n$-separated net of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$.
  Let $x \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal separated net outside B(A,4 lambda^n)

nodes.name: Case x near A: find a nearby net point
nodes.statement:
Suppose there exists $y \in A$ such that $\rho(x,y) < 4\lambda^n$.
  As $\lambda < 1/4$, we get by \eqref{e:A-spread-out} that the number of balls $\{B_\rho(p,4 \lambda^n)\}_{p \in A}$ 
  that intersect $B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1})$ is at most 2.  This, together with \eqref{e:small-lambda}, gives that
  \[
    B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n) \neq \emptyset.
  \]
  Thus, there exists some $z \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$.
  As $\{x_i\}$ is also a $4\lambda^n$ covering of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, 
  we get that there exists some $x_i$ such that $\rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n$.  Altogether, we get that
  \[
    \rho(x,x_i) \leq \rho(x,y) + \rho(y,z) + \rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n + \lambda^{n-1} + 4 \lambda^n 
    =  \left(8 +  \frac{1}{\lambda} \right)\lambda^n.
  \]
nodes.statement_short: Case x near A: find a nearby net point

nodes.name: Case x far from A: net covers
nodes.statement: In the case when $x \notin B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, we are also done as the set  $\{x_i\}$ is a $4\lambda^n$-cover of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Case x far from A: net covers

nodes.name: Removing a non decreasing-increasing level pattern
nodes.statement: Suppose ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\mathbb N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$ Then the itinerary ${\bf x}' = (x_0',\dots,x_{N-2}') \in {\mathcal I}_A$ where \[ x_k' = \begin{cases} x_k & k \in \{0,\dots,j+1\}, \\ x_{k+2} & k \in \{j+2,\dots,N-2\}, \end{cases} \] satisfies $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$.
assumptions: ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\mathbb N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$
conclusions: satisfies $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.label: lma:weak-id

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Show the middle walk-fly-walk can be replaced by one walk, using the shortcut condition (3.1) after checking the endpoints lie outside the shortcut ball.

nodes.name: Endpoints unchanged; consider the subitinerary y
nodes.statement:
That $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ is obvious from construction.  
  Consider the subitinerary ${\bf y} = (x_{j+1},x_{j+2},x_{j+3},x_{j+4})$.
nodes.statement_short: Endpoints unchanged; consider the subitinerary y

nodes.name: Claim: one walk is cheaper than y
nodes.statement:
We claim that $c(x_{j+1},x_{j+4}) \leq c({\bf y})$, which proves the lemma.
  Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{j+2},x_{j+3})$ was found in $B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.
  Then 
  $n= L (  x_{j+2},x_{j+3}  )$. 
  We claim that  
  $x_{j+1},x_{j+4} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.  Indeed, by assumption, $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) \leq n$.
  So first suppose $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$.  Then
  $x$ was found in the complement of
  \[
    B(x_j,2\lambda^n) \cup B(x_{j+1},2\lambda^n).
  \]
  If instead $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$, then let  $y \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which 
  the shortcut $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ was found
  in $B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$.
  We may assume that $x\neq y$, otherwise $\{x_j,x_{j+1}\}=\{x_{j+2},x_{j+3}\}$ and the claim is obvious.
Hence,   we have that $\rho(x,y) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and so
  \[
    B_\rho(x,\lambda^n) \cap B_\rho(y,\lambda^n) = \emptyset.
  \]
  As $x_{j+1} \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$, we get that $x_{j+1} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.
  A similar argument holds for $x_{j+4}$.
  Thus, we have that the claim follows from 
  \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption2} if we set $x_i=x$, $q_{i,1} = x_{j+2}$, $q_{i,2} = x_{j+3}$, $p_1 = x_{j+1}$, and $p_2 = x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: one walk is cheaper than y

nodes.name: Introduce the centre x of the middle shortcut
nodes.statement:
Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{j+2},x_{j+3})$ was found in $B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.
  Then 
  $n= L (  x_{j+2},x_{j+3}  )$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the centre x of the middle shortcut

nodes.name: Claim: the outer points avoid the shortcut ball
nodes.statement:
We claim that  
  $x_{j+1},x_{j+4} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.  Indeed, by assumption, $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) \leq n$.
  So first suppose $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$.  Then
  $x$ was found in the complement of
  \[
    B(x_j,2\lambda^n) \cup B(x_{j+1},2\lambda^n).
  \]
  If instead $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$, then let  $y \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which 
  the shortcut $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ was found
  in $B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$.
  We may assume that $x\neq y$, otherwise $\{x_j,x_{j+1}\}=\{x_{j+2},x_{j+3}\}$ and the claim is obvious.
Hence,   we have that $\rho(x,y) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and so
  \[
    B_\rho(x,\lambda^n) \cap B_\rho(y,\lambda^n) = \emptyset.
  \]
  As $x_{j+1} \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$, we get that $x_{j+1} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.
  A similar argument holds for $x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the outer points avoid the shortcut ball

nodes.name: Case lower level: x chosen away from them
nodes.statement:
Indeed, by assumption, $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) \leq n$.
  So first suppose $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$.  Then
  $x$ was found in the complement of
  \[
    B(x_j,2\lambda^n) \cup B(x_{j+1},2\lambda^n).
  \]
nodes.statement_short: Case lower level: x chosen away from them

nodes.name: Case equal level: separated balls
nodes.statement:
If instead $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$, then let  $y \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which 
  the shortcut $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ was found
  in $B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$.
  We may assume that $x\neq y$, otherwise $\{x_j,x_{j+1}\}=\{x_{j+2},x_{j+3}\}$ and the claim is obvious.
Hence,   we have that $\rho(x,y) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and so
  \[
    B_\rho(x,\lambda^n) \cap B_\rho(y,\lambda^n) = \emptyset.
  \]
  As $x_{j+1} \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$, we get that $x_{j+1} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.
  A similar argument holds for $x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Case equal level: separated balls

nodes.name: Apply (3.1)
nodes.statement:
Thus, we have that the claim follows from 
  \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption2} if we set $x_i=x$, $q_{i,1} = x_{j+2}$, $q_{i,2} = x_{j+3}$, $p_1 = x_{j+1}$, and $p_2 = x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply (3.1)

nodes.name: Reduction to decreasing-increasing itineraries with bounded level multiplicity
nodes.statement: For any ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A$, there exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$, and \begin{equation} \# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N. \end{equation} Moreover, ${\bf x}$ and ${\bf x}'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Every alternating itinerary can be replaced by one in I* with no greater cost, same endpoints and first/last shortcuts, each level used at most 4 times.
conclusions: there exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$, and \begin{equation} \# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N. \end{equation}
${\bf x}$ and ${\bf x}'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.
nodes.label: lma:multiplicity

nodes.name: Level multiplicity bound (3.4)
nodes.statement: \# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N.
nodes.label: e:4-bound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Given an initial ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A$, we iterate Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} until we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ for which there are no indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. As the length of the itinerary shrinks by 2 with each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, we get that we have to stop after some finite number of iterations. It is elementary to see that if $L_{\bf x'} : \{0,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb N$ satisfies $$L_{{\bf x}'}(i+1) < \max (L_{{\bf x}'}(i),L_{{\bf x}'}(i+2)), \qquad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,n-2\},$$ then $L_{{\bf x}'}$ is decreasing-increasing, which means that ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$. Now suppose $\# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) > 4$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$. As ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we get that there exists some $i \in 2\mathbb N$ so that $$L(x_i,x_{i+1}) = L(x_{i+2},x_{i+3}) = L(x_{i+4},x_{i+5}).$$ But this contradicts the assumption that ${\bf x}'$ does not have any indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. Finally, since each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} keeps the first and last shortcut of ${\bf x}$ unchanged the resulting itinerary ${\bf x}'$ has the same first and last shortcut as ${\bf x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Lemma 3.2 until no index satisfies its hypothesis; then the level function is decreasing-increasing and has multiplicity at most 4.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: The validity of the triangle inequality follows from the definition of the distance as defined in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Symmetry is due to the symmetry of the cost function. What needs to be checked is that $x \ne y$ implies $d(x,y)>0$. In order to show this, suppose that $x,y \in X$ with $\rho(x,y)>0$. Let $n \in \mathbb N$ be such that \[ 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \le \frac12\rho(x,y). \] Let $(\alpha_n)$ be the sequence of positive numbers used to construct the cost function in Section~\ref{sec:construction}. Consider the positive number \[ \varepsilon := \min\left(\frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1}, \frac14\rho(x,y)\right). \] Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq d(x,y) + \varepsilon$, and $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} (remember that using stationary walks every itinerary can be modified to be an alternating itinerary of no greater cost, because of triangle inequality). On the one hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) = \emptyset$, then the alternating itinerary does not have shortcuts at odd steps and it has them at even steps only of level greater that $n$ and with multiplicity at most $4$. Hence, we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(x,y) & \ge & c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge \sum_{j \text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \varepsilon \ge \rho(x,y) - \sum_{j \text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \frac14\rho(x,y)\\ & \ge & \frac34\rho(x,y) - 4 \sum_{k=n}^\infty 2\lambda^k \ge \frac34\rho(x,y) - 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \ge \frac14\rho(x,y) > 0, \end{eqnarray*} where we used that a point in a shortcuts at level $k$ has $\rho$-distance less than $ \lambda^k$ from the center of the ball in which the shortcut was found. On the other hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) \ne \emptyset$, then, if $(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell)$ is a shortcut at level $l<n$ of ${\bf x}$, we have \[ d(x,y) \ge c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) - \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} \ge \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0, \] where we used that $ c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) = \alpha_l \rho(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) \geq \alpha_l \lambda^l.$ In both cases $d(x,y) > 0$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Positivity: take a near-optimal itinerary in I* and split on whether it uses a low-level shortcut; geometric sum bounds the high-level shortcuts.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: Suppose to the contrary that there exist two disjoint $(q_1,q_2), (\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ with \begin{equation} L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n \end{equation} and $q_1,\tilde q_1 \in B_d(x,r)$. Then \[ d(q_1,\tilde q_1) \le d(q_1,x) + d(x,\tilde q_1) < 2r \le 2\lambda^n. \] Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $x_0=q_1,$ $x_N=\tilde q_1$ and \begin{equation} c({\bf x}) < 2\lambda^n. \end{equation} We may assume that $N$ is odd, up to adding a stationary walk at the end. Hence the slightly longer itinerary ${\bf y}=(q_2,q_2,q_1,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2)$ is an alternating itinerary. By applying Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} to ${\bf y}$ we know that there exists $ {\bf y}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $ c( {\bf y}') \le c( {\bf y}), $ where $ {\rm Ext}( {\bf y}') ={\rm Ext} ( {\bf y}) $. Notice that, since the construction in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} keeps the the first and last shortcuts stay the same, we have that ${\bf y}'$ is of the form \[{\bf y}' = (q_2,q_2,q_1,x'_1,\dots,x'_{N'}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) .\] We conclude that the itinerary ${\bf x}$ may be replaced with no extra cost by an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ that is decreasing-increasing and, due to \eqref{e:shortcut-lower-bnds}, we have $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([n,\infty]) = \emptyset$. We remark that the itinerary ${\bf x}'$ cannot have only stationary walks, i.e., there is some $j \in 2\mathbb Z$ so that $x'_j \neq x'_{j+1}$. Indeed, otherwise the itinerary cannot move away from $\{q_1,q_2\}$, since distinct shortcuts are separated. Hence, there are two distinct shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Set $k_1:= L(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$ $k_2:= L(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Recall that $k_1,k_2<n$. Let $a, b$ are the centers of the balls in which the shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$ were found with radii $\lambda^{k_1}$ and $\lambda^{k_2}$, respectively. Let us distinguish two cases. Assume first that $k_1=k_2=:k$, so that $a$ and $ b$ are $4\lambda^{k}$ separated. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(a,b) -\rho(a,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k} - \lambda^{k}- \lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^n. \] Suppose now $k_1\neq k_2$, say that $k_1< k_2$, the other case is similar. Recall that $b$ was found outside $B(x'_j,4\lambda^{k_2})$ in the construction of the shortcuts. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(b,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k_2} - \lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^n. \] In either case we have \[ c({\bf x}) \ge c({\bf x}') \ge \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge 2\lambda^n, \] which is in contradiction with \eqref{eq:q1q1small}.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: a cheap itinerary between two distinct low-level shortcuts must walk at least 2 lambda^n between separated shortcuts.

nodes.name: Ball inclusions between d and rho

conclusions: there exist $y_1,y_2 \in X$ such that \begin{equation} B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right). \end{equation}
nodes.label: lma:inclusions

nodes.name: Ball inclusions (3.7)
nodes.statement: B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right).
nodes.label: eq:inclusions

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$. Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})=(x,z)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$. Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \mathbb N \cup\{0\}$ be such that \[ \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n. \] By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ and \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset. \end{equation} If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$. Now \[ B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r). \] Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even. Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = n}^\infty \lambda^k = 2r + 8\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $ \lambda^{n+1} \le r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds.
nodes.statement_short: First inclusion from d <= rho; second by cases r >= 1 and r < 1, using Lemma 3.5 to isolate the one large shortcut and a geometric sum for the rest.

nodes.name: Unique big jump (3.8)
nodes.statement: L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset.

nodes.name: First inclusion from d <= rho
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$.
nodes.statement_short: First inclusion from d <= rho

nodes.name: Second inclusion
nodes.statement:
Let us show the second inclusion.  Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$.
 By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})=(x,z)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Then
 \begin{eqnarray*}
  \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le
   \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\
   & \le &  c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le  \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r,
 \end{eqnarray*}
 since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$.
 
 Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \mathbb N \cup\{0\}$ be such that
 \[
   \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n.
 \]
 By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ and
 \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset.
 \end{equation}
 If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$.
 Now 
 \[
  B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r).
 \]
 Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity}
 there exists 
 ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, 
 $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$.
 By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain
 the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$.
 Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even. 
 
 Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we have
 \begin{eqnarray*}
   \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.3 (3): no biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement:
Let $A\subseteq X$ be such that $\mathcal H^4_{\rho}(A)>0$. 
Our aim is to show that $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
For this purpose take a density-point $x$ of $A$. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $r_\epsilon > 0$
such that
\[
 B_\rho(x,r) \subset B_\rho(A,\epsilon r), \qquad \text{for all }r \in (0,r_\epsilon).
\]
Now, for all $n \in \mathbb N$ there exists $(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) \in {\mathcal S}$ with $L(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) = n$ such that
\[
 \{q_{n,1},q_{n,2}\} \subset B_\rho(x,2c_E\lambda^n).
\]
If $3c_E\lambda^n < r_\epsilon$, there exist $x_{n,1},x_{n,2} \in A$ such that 
\[
\rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n
\qquad \text{and}\qquad
\rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n.
\]
Then
\[
 \rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) \ge \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) - \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) - \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})
 \ge \lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n
\]
and
\begin{eqnarray*}
 d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) & \le & d(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + d(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + d(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\
         & \le & \alpha_n \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\
         & \le & 2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n.
\end{eqnarray*}
Therefore we have
\[
 \frac{d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})}{\rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})} \le \frac{2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n}{\lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n} = \frac{2\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon}{\lambda-6c_E\epsilon}.
\]
As $\alpha_n \to 0$, by letting $n$ be sufficiently large and $\epsilon$ be sufficiently small, we get that $\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon$ is sufficently small and so
the distances $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.

nodes.statement: We will verify that the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold in the Heisenberg group with $\lambda = \frac12$. Let $p \in \mathbb H$ and $r > 0$. By left-translation invariance of the distance $d_b$ in $\mathbb H$ we may assume that $p = (0,0,0)$. Take $q_1 = (0,0,0)$ and $q_2 = (0,0,r^2/4)$. Now let $p_1,p_2 \notin B(0,r)$. Since $d_b(q_1,q_2) = \sqrt{r^2/4} = r/2$, by the triangle inequality we have that $d_b(p_1,q_1) \ge r/2$ and $d_b(p_2,q_2) \ge r/2$. Write $p_1 = (x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $p_2 = (x_2,y_2,z_2)$. Then the equation for the box distance is given by \eqref{eq:box:dist}. Trivially, we have \[ |x_1-x_2| \le |x_1| + |x_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2) \] and \[ |y_2-y_1| \le |y_1| + |y_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2). \] By using the triangle inequality and the estimate $r^2/4 \le d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)$ we also get \begin{eqnarray*} \left|z_1-z_2-\frac12(x_1y_2-x_2y_1) \right| & \le & |z_1|+|z_2-\frac14r^2|+\frac14r^2 +\frac12|x_1||y_2| + \frac12|x_2||y_1|\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2+d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & & +\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+2d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2\\ & = & \left(d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2)\right)^2. \end{eqnarray*} Thus we have \[ d_b(p_1,p_2) \le d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2) \] as required by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.

Then the snowflaked metric space $(X,d^\delta)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Consequently, there exists a distance $d'$ on $X$ such that $d' \le d^\delta$, $(X,d')$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular, and for any $A\subseteq X$ with $\mathcal H^{Q/\delta}_{d^\delta}(A)>0$, we have that $d'$ and $d^\delta$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: First of all, it is trivial that $(X,d^\delta)$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular. Let us then check the assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Since $(X,d)$ is $Q$-regular, there exists $C > 1$ such that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q(B_d(x,r)) \le Cr^Q \end{equation} for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$. We shall set $\lambda:= (2C)^{-2\delta/Q}(1-\delta)^\delta$. Take $p \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$. Define $q_1 = p$ and take \[ q_2 \in B_d(p,(1-\delta)r^\frac{1}{\delta}) \setminus B_d(p, (2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta) r^\frac{1}{\delta}). \] Such $q_2$ exists since the annulus from where the point is taken has positive measure by \eqref{eq:ahlfors} and is hence non-empty. In particular, $q_1, q_2\in B_{d^\delta} (p,r)$ and \[ d(q_1,q_2)^\delta \ge \left((2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta)\right)^\delta r = \lambda r. \] Now, take $p_1,p_2 \notin B_d\left(p,r^\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$. We get that $$ d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2) \geq \delta r^{1/\delta},$$ and so $$d(q_1,q_2) \leq \left( 1 - \delta\right) r^{1/\delta} \leq \left( \frac{1}{\delta} - 1 \right) \min(d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2)).$$ First assume that $d(p_1,q_1) \le d(p_2,q_2)$. Then we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(p_1,p_2)^\delta & \le & (d(p_1,q_1)+d(q_1,q_2)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta \\ & \le & ((1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta\\ & \le & d(p_2,q_2)^\delta + \delta(1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)d(p_2,q_2)^{1-\delta} \\ & \le & d(p_1,q_1)^\delta + d(p_2,q_2)^\delta \end{eqnarray*} verifying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption}. In the penultimate inequality, we used the fact that $x \mapsto x^\delta$ is concave so that the higher order terms of the Taylor expansion is always negative. An analogous calculation takes care of the case $d(p_2,q_2) \leq d(p_1,q_1)$.

nodes.name: Proof that K has nonempty interior
nodes.statement:
Let us show that $K$ has nonempty interior. 
 First of all, the horizontal projection of the iterated function system has the unit square as the attractor.
 Secondly, since the dilation and the group operation commute, we may consider separately the horizontal and vertical components
 of the iterated function system. This way we see that
 \begin{equation} K = \{(x,y,z+t) \,:\, (x,y,z) \in \widetilde K, t \in [0,1]\},
 \end{equation}
 where $\widetilde K$ is the attractor of the horizontal component that is realized as the attractor of the system
 \[
  \{S_{i,j,0}\,:\, i,j \in \{0,1\}\}.
 \]
 The set $\widetilde K$ has the form
 \begin{equation} \widetilde K = \overline{\{(x,y,\varphi(x,y))\,:\,(x,y)\in [0,1]^2\}}
 \end{equation}
 with some Borel function $\varphi \colon [0,1]^2 \to \mathbb R$. Observe that $\varphi$ is bounded since $K$ is compact.
 Also, since $0$ is the fixed point of $S_{0,0,0}$ and $S_{i,j,0}(\widetilde K)$ do not contain $0$ if $i\ne 0$ or $j \ne 0$, 
 the function $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the IFS into horizontal and vertical parts: K is a vertical unit thickening of a graph over the unit square, continuous at 0.

nodes.name: Compositions S_i for multi-indices
nodes.statement:
For a multi-index  
$\mathtt{i}=
 (i_1,...,i_k)  \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, we shall use the standard notation
$S_{\mathtt{i}}$ for the composition \[ 
S_{\mathtt{i}}:=  S_{i_1} \circ S_{i_2} \circ \cdots \circ S_{i_k}.\]
With $k=0$ we interpret $\{1,\dots,16\}^k$ to consist of only one element, call it $\emptyset$, and $S_\emptyset$ is then understood
to be the identity map.

nodes.name: Self-similar level n shortcuts in K
nodes.statement:
We define the shortcuts at level $n$ as 
 \[
   {\mathcal S}_n := \{(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,\frac1{64}))\,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\}.
 \]

nodes.name: Levels of the self-similar shortcuts
nodes.statement: We also set $L(x,y) = n$ for $(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_n$.  Note that levels start from $n = 3$.

nodes.name: Total set of self-similar shortcuts
nodes.statement:
We then define the total set of shortcuts as
 \[
   {\mathcal S} := \bigcup_{n=3}^\infty {\mathcal S}_n.
 \]

nodes.name: Zero cost of self-similar shortcuts
nodes.statement: Define the cost as $c(x,y) = 0$ for all $(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}$.

nodes.name: Horizontal projection pi
nodes.statement:
In the following lemmas we will use the map
  \[\pi : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to \mathbb R^2\]
  that is  the projection onto the $xy$-plane 
   and is a $1$-Lipschitz homomorphism, when we endow $\mathbb R^2$ with the $\ell_\infty$-distance.

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centres avoid earlier shortcuts
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$, we have \[ \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \cap \left( \bigcup_{m < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_m} B_{d_b}(\{x,y\},2^{-n+2}) \right) = \emptyset. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$. Note that for each $k$ we have that \[ \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \mathbb R\}) = A_k. \] As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that \[ A_n \cap B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset. \] But this follows from the geometry of $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Note that we need the sets $B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.
nodes.statement_short: Project to the plane by the 1-Lipschitz pi and use the geometry of dyadic centres in the sup norm.

nodes.name: Projections of shortcut points are dyadic centres
nodes.statement:
Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$.  Note that for each $k$ we have that
   \[
     \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \mathbb R\}) = A_k.
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Projections of shortcut points are dyadic centres

nodes.name: Reduce to a planar statement
nodes.statement:
As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that
   \[
     A_n \cap B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset.
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a planar statement

nodes.name: Planar geometry of dyadic centres
nodes.statement: But this follows from the geometry of $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$.  Note that we need the sets $B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centres are separated
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$ the set \[ A:= \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \] is $2^{-n+2}$-separated (note: $2^{-n+2} = 4 \cdot 2^{-n}$, which is needed for the construction).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: As shown in the previous lemma, the image of $A$ under $\pi$ is precisely the centers of the dyadic subcubes of $[0,1]$ of level $n-3$. Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$. Then \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}. \] Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$. Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$, where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether the projections differ: horizontal separation, or vertical separation of 4-adic centres.

nodes.name: Projections are dyadic centres (previous lemma)
nodes.statement:
As shown in the previous lemma, the image of 

$A$
   under $\pi$ is precisely the centers of the dyadic subcubes of $[0,1]$ of level $n-3$.
nodes.statement_short: Projections are dyadic centres (previous lemma)

nodes.name: Case different projections
nodes.statement:
Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$.  Then
   \[
     d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}.
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Case different projections

nodes.name: Case same projection: vertical separation
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$.  Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$,
   where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. 
    Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so

     d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} .
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Case same projection: vertical separation

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centres cover K
nodes.statement: There exists some absolute constant $c_E > 0$ so that \begin{equation} K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lma:K-c1

nodes.name: Covering of K by balls (5.4)
nodes.statement: K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3.
nodes.label: e:K-ball-ind

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction. As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough. Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$. Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get \begin{eqnarray*} K& = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\ & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1}) \end{eqnarray*} Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n using the self-similarity K = union S_i(K).

nodes.name: Base case n = 3 by boundedness
nodes.statement:
We prove the claim by induction.
  As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Base case n = 3 by boundedness

nodes.name: Inductive step via self-similarity
nodes.statement:
Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$.
  Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get
  \begin{eqnarray*}
    K&  = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\
    & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1})
  \end{eqnarray*}
  Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via self-similarity

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 1: (H,d_b) looks down on (K,d)
nodes.statement:
By Remark~\ref{rmk:zerocost} taking zero costs for shortcuts is allowed.
 From the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} we see that $\lambda = \frac12$ works in the Heisenberg group. 
 
 Now the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold for the constructed distance $d$.
 That is, the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz, 
 but not biLipschitz on any set of positive measure, and the space $(K,d)$ is Ahlfors regular.
 In particular, $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$. In order to show that $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ is not minimal in 
 looking down, we still need to prove that $(K,d)$ is a BPI space and that
 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1.3 to the self-similar zero-cost shortcuts in K: id:(K,d_b)->(K,d) is Lipschitz, so (H,d_b) looks down on (K,d).

nodes.name: Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 hold in (K,d)
nodes.statement:
Note that Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} holds in $(K,d)$ as its proof, as well as the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, only require that $\mathcal{N}_{n+1} \cap B_{d_b}(\mathcal{N}_n,4 \lambda^n) = \emptyset$, which holds for 
  the construction of $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Short walks next to low-level shortcuts
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ and $n = \min \{k \in \mathbb N : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}$. There exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$, and for any $j \in \mathbb N$ such that $\min (L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}),L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})) = m < n$, then \[ d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \leq 2 \lambda^m. \]
nodes.label: lma:small-walks

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_{\bf x}$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$. Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$. Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$. Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$. If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality. Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in ${\bf x}$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points. We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary ${\bf x}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace any long walk adjacent to a low-level shortcut using the shortcut inequality, and iterate.

nodes.name: WLOG the level function is still decreasing
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_{\bf x}$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$.  Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG the level function is still decreasing

nodes.name: A long walk can be removed by the shortcut inequality
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$.  Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$.  If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality.  Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in ${\bf x}$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points.
nodes.statement_short: A long walk can be removed by the shortcut inequality

nodes.statement: We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary ${\bf x}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate

nodes.name: Length |i| of a multi-index
nodes.statement: In this section we write $|\mathtt{i}|=k$ if $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$.

nodes.name: Near-optimal itineraries stay near S_i(K)
nodes.statement: There exists some $C > 0$ so that for all multi-indices ${\mathtt{i}}$, for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_n\in B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement:
We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \mathbb N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary ${ f x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that  egin{enumerate} \item $c({ f x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\mathrm{Ext}({ f x}) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad  orall k \in \mathbb N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_{ f x}^{-1}(k) 
eq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${ f x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({ f x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({ f x}) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$. The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$. Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \mathbb N$ be the minimal even number such that  egin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and  egin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation} As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that  egin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation} By an application of Lemma~ef{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary ${ f x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. We then apply Lemma~ef{lma:small-walks} on ${ f x}$ (and still calling the result ${ f x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied. Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$. Then \[ c({ f x}) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] a contradiction. Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied. Now suppose $L_{ f x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) 
eq \emptyset$. Suppose first that $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$. Then as ${ f x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) 
otin {\mathcal S}$ such that \[ c({ f x}) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] which is a contradiction. Now suppose that $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$. Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$. Then we have by the triangle inequality  egin{multline*} d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \ - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*). \end{multline*} We have that  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} 
otag \ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray} Together with the fourth property, we get that \[ (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}. \] But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim six properties of a near-optimal itinerary for deep cylinders; prove them by contradiction using Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4 and tail sums; small cylinders handled by finiteness.

nodes.name: Small tails (5.8)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} \notag \\ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}.
nodes.label: e:small-tails

nodes.name: Claim: six properties for deep cylinders
nodes.statement:
We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \mathbb N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that
   \begin{enumerate}
    \item $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$,
    \item $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$,
    \item $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N$,
    \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that
      \[
        m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\},
      \]
    \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd,
    \item $L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$.
   \end{enumerate}
   If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with  $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and 
   \[
     \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}
   \]
   for some $C$ depending on $M$.  The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality
   and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: six properties for deep cylinders

nodes.name: The claim gives total d_b-length C 2^{-|i|}
nodes.statement:
If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with  $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and 
   \[
     \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|}
   \]
   for some $C$ depending on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: The claim gives total d_b-length C 2^{-|i|}

nodes.name: Lemma follows; finitely many short multi-indices
nodes.statement:
The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality
   and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma follows; finitely many short multi-indices

nodes.name: Proof of the claim
nodes.statement:
Let us prove the claim.  Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1}.
   Let $M \in \mathbb N$ be the minimal even number such that
   \begin{equation}
    2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation}
   and
   \begin{equation}
     2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation}
   As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$,   if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that
   \begin{equation}
     d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation}

   By an application of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties.  We then apply Lemma~\ref{lma:small-walks} on ${\bf x}$ (and still calling the result ${\bf x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied.

   Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$.  Then
   \[
     c({\bf x}) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y),
   \]
   a contradiction.  Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied.
   
   Now suppose $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) \neq \emptyset$.  Suppose first that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$.  Then as ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \notin {\mathcal S}$ such that
   \[
     c({\bf x}) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y),
   \]
   which is a contradiction.

   Now suppose that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$.  Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$.  Then we have by the triangle inequality
   \begin{multline*}
     d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \\
     - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*).
   \end{multline*}
   We have that
   \begin{eqnarray}
     \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} \notag \\
     \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray}
   Together with the fourth property, we get that
   \[
     (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}.
   \]
   But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proof of the claim

nodes.statement_short: Fix c_E and choose M

Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4 give properties 1-4

We then apply Lemma~\ref{lma:small-walks} on ${\bf x}$ (and still calling the result ${\bf x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied.
