nodes.name: Property 5 by contradiction
nodes.statement:
Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$.  Then
   \[
     c({\bf x}) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y),
   \]
   a contradiction.  Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Property 5 by contradiction

nodes.name: Property 6: case of two low-level shortcuts
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) \neq \emptyset$.  Suppose first that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$.  Then as ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \notin {\mathcal S}$ such that
   \[
     c({\bf x}) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y),
   \]
   which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Property 6: case of two low-level shortcuts

nodes.name: Property 6: case of one low-level shortcut
nodes.statement:
Now suppose that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$.  Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$.  Then we have by the triangle inequality
   \begin{multline*}
     d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \\
     - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*).
   \end{multline*}
   We have that
   \begin{eqnarray}
     \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} \notag \\
     \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray}
   Together with the fourth property, we get that
   \[
     (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}.
   \]
   But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Property 6: case of one low-level shortcut

nodes.name: Optimal itineraries inside S_i(K) for a deep sub-cylinder
nodes.statement: There exists some multi-index $\mathtt{j}$ such that the following property holds. For any $\epsilon > 0$, $k \in \mathbb N$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, and any two $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_N \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
nodes.label: lma:j-defn

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma. As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$. As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K. \] Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$. Then there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of ${\bf x}$ is contained \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K). \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose a cylinder S_j(K) whose C-neighbourhood lies in the interior of K; rescale by S_i and apply the previous lemma.

nodes.name: Choose j with neighbourhood inside K
nodes.statement:
Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma.  As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$.  As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that
   \[
    B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K.
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose j with neighbourhood inside K

nodes.name: Previous lemma keeps itinerary inside S_i(K)
nodes.statement:
Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$.  Then there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of ${\bf x}$ is contained
   \[
     B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K).
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Previous lemma keeps itinerary inside S_i(K)

nodes.name: Exact scaling of d on S_j(K) under the similitudes
nodes.statement: Let $\mathtt{j}$ be from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}. Then for all $k \in \mathbb N$ and $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, we have that \begin{equation} d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Scaling of d (5.9)
nodes.statement: d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K).
nodes.label: e:j-invariance

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.7
nodes.statement: If ${\bf x}$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$ by the properties of the shortcuts. Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$. For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$. Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to ${\bf x}$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$. Thus, \[ d(x,y) \leq c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x}) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)). \] Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Push itineraries forward and back by S_i; Lemma 5.6 keeps optimal itineraries inside S_i(K).

nodes.name: Upper bound by pushing itineraries forward
nodes.statement: If ${\bf x}$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$ by the properties of the shortcuts.  Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound by pushing itineraries forward

nodes.name: Lower bound via Lemma 5.6 and pulling back
nodes.statement:
For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.  Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to ${\bf x}$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$.  Thus,
   \[
     d(x,y) \leq c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x}) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)).
   \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound via Lemma 5.6 and pulling back

nodes.name: Let epsilon -> 0
nodes.statement: Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Let epsilon -> 0

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 2: (K,d) is BPI
nodes.statement:
We can now prove that $K$ is BPI.
 Let $\mathtt{j}$ be the multi-index from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}, $p_1,p_2 \in K$, and $0 < r_1,r_2 < \operatorname{diam}(K)$.
 Now there exist two multi-indices $\mathtt{i_1},\mathtt{i_2}$ such that $\operatorname{diam}(S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K)) \ge c r_j$
 and $S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K) \subset B(p_j,r_j)$ for $j \in \{1,2\}$. Define $A = S_{\mathtt{i_1}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)) \subset B(p_1,r_1)$.
 Then the map $f \colon A \to B(p_2,r_2)$ defined as $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2}\circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$ satisfies
 \[
   d(f(p),f(q)) \overset{\eqref{e:j-invariance}}{=} 2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q \in A.
 \]
 Since $\mathcal{H}_d^4(A) \ge c\mathcal{H}_d^4(B(p_1,r_1))$ for some $c$ depending only on $\mathtt{j}$ and $2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}$ is comparable to
 $r_2/r_1$, we are done with showing that $(K,d)$ is BPI.
nodes.statement_short: Map one cylinder S_{i1}(S_j(K)) onto another by S_{i2} S_{i1}^{-1}, which is a similarity for d by Lemma 5.7.

 Now there exist two multi-indices $\mathtt{i_1},\mathtt{i_2}$ such that $\operatorname{diam}(S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K)) \ge c r_j$

nodes.name: f is a similarity by (5.9)
nodes.statement:
Then the map $f \colon A \to B(p_2,r_2)$ defined as $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2}\circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$ satisfies
 \[
   d(f(p),f(q)) \overset{\eqref{e:j-invariance}}{=} 2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q \in A.
 \]

nodes.name: A is big, so (K,d) is BPI
nodes.statement:
Since $\mathcal{H}_d^4(A) \ge c\mathcal{H}_d^4(B(p_1,r_1))$ for some $c$ depending only on $\mathtt{j}$ and $2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}$ is comparable to

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 3: (K,d) does not look down on (H,d_b)
nodes.statement:
By contradiction, suppose that $(K,d)$ does look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$. 
 Then there would exist a closed set $A \subset K$ and a 
 Lipschitz map $f \colon (A,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\mathcal{H}^4(f(A))>0$. Since $d \le d_b$, also 
 $f \colon (A,d_b) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Then $f$ is Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere in $A$.
 Moreover, the Pansu-differential $Df(x)$ is bijective on a set $A' \subset A$ of positive measure by the area formula:
 \[
  0 < \mathcal{H}^4(f(A)) \overset{\eqref{e:area-formula}}{\le} \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x).
 \]
 Since for all $n,m \in \mathbb N$ the set
 \[
  B_{n,m} = K \setminus \bigcup_{k = n}^\infty \bigcup_{ \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k}S_{\mathtt{i}}(K\cap B_{d_b}(0,\frac1m))
 \]
 has $\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}$-measure zero as a porous set, the set
 \begin{equation} A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m}
 \end{equation}
 has positive measure. Let $x \in A''$ be a density point of $A''$.
 Since $x \in A''$, by the definition \eqref{eq:Adef} there exists a sequence $(n_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ of integers with
 $n_m \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ and a sequence of multi-indices $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $|\mathtt{i}_m| = n_m$ such that
 $x \in S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(K)$ for all $m \in \mathbb N$ and
 \[
  d_b(x,x_m)< \frac1m 2^{-{n_m}} ,
 \]
 for all $m \in \mathbb N$, where $x_m = S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$.
 
 




 
 Let $K_m = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(x^{-1}A)\cap K$. Then the functions $f_m \colon (K_m,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ defined as
 \[
   f_m(p) = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)))
 \]
 satisfy 
 
 \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}
   d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & =  d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\
   & =  2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\
   & \le  2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\
   & \le  L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\
   & =  L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\
   & \le  L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right),
  \end{aligned}
 \end{equation}
 where the first inequality follows from the fact that $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and the second inequality from the fact that
 \[
   S_{\mathtt{i}_n}({\mathcal S}) \subset {\mathcal S}.
 \]
 Notice that 
 \begin{equation} d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0
 \end{equation}
 as $m \to \infty$ since $d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x),0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$.
 The convergence in \eqref{eq:errorterm} holds uniformly for $p \in K$ by the compactness of $K$.
 
 Since $x$ is a density point of $A''$ and hence of $A$, we have that 
 for all $p \in K$ there exists a sequence $(p_m)_{m=1}^\infty$  with $p_m \in K_{n_m}$ and $d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$
 as $m \to \infty$. Along this sequence 
 by the fact that $Df(x)$ is homogeneous we get 
 
 \begin{eqnarray*}
   d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) & = &
   d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_{n_m}))),\delta_{2^{{n_m}}}(Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))))\\
   &=&2^{n_m} d_b(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m)),Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))) \to 0,
 \end{eqnarray*}
 as $m \to \infty$. 
 Hence also
 \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}
   d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m))
    + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0,
  \end{aligned}
 \end{equation}
 as $m \to \infty$.
 
 
 Combining the estimates \eqref{eq:fmdestimate}, \eqref{eq:fm_estimate} and \eqref{eq:errorterm} with the fact that 
 $d(p_m,p) \leq d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ we get
 \begin{eqnarray*}
   d_b(Df(x)(p),Df(x)(q)) & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\
   & & \hspace{5.7cm}+ d_b(f_m(p_m),f_m(q_m))\\
   & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\

   & &\hspace{3.59cm} + L\left(d(p_m,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,q_m)\right)\\
   & \rightarrow & L d(p,q), \qquad \text{as }m \to \infty.
 \end{eqnarray*}
 Hence $Df(x)$ is also Lipschitz from $(K,d)$ to $(\mathbb H, d_b)$.
 Since $Df(x) \colon (\mathbb H, d_b) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is biLipschitz, also the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K, d)
 \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is Lipschitz, but we have shown that this is not the case in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement:
Since $ d_{cc}$ is biLipschitz equivalent to the box distance, up to multiplying $d$ by a constant we assume that 
$d \le d_{b}$.



 Using the Baire Category
Theorem one can show that there exists $L>1$ such that,  if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant, see
 \cite[Lemma 6.7]{LeDonne1}.
 Suppose that the claim of the theorem is not true. 
 Hence, by the left-biLipschitz invariance of the distances,
 for all $N\in \mathbb N  $ there exists a point $p \in B_{d_b}(0,\frac1{2N})$
 with $d_b(0,p) > LN d(0,p)$.
 




 
 Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that
 \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)
  \subset B_d(0,2 r_N)
  . 
 \end{eqnarray}�
 Indeed,
 if $q\in 
 B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then 
\begin{eqnarray*}
d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\
&\leq &   LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q)
\\
&\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2  < 2r_N.
\end{eqnarray*}
Moreover, for $i < j<N$, we have that
 \[
   d_b(p^i,p^j) = d_b(0,p^{j-i}) \geq d_b(0,p) = r_N.
 \]
  
 
 Let $\{q_i\}_{i \in I_N}$ be a maximal $4r_N$-separated net of points with respect to distance $d$ in $B_{d_b}(0,1)$.
 First,
 by \eqref{ciccio} for all $i \in I_N$ we have that 
$
\{B_{d_b}(q_i p^n,\frac12 r_N)  \}_{n=0}^{N} $

is a disjointed collection of subsets of
$   B_{d_b}(q_i,2r_N)
 $.
 Second, 
 $\{B_d(q_i,2r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ is a disjointed collection of subsets of
 $B_{d_b}(0,2)$.
 Hence 
 
















 
 \[
 \#I_N N \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))
  \leq
  \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))
  .
 \]
Since $\{B_d(q_i,8r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ covers $B_{d_b}(0,1)$, by  definition of Hausdorff measure we deduce
 \begin{eqnarray*}
  \mathcal{H}_d^4(B_{d_b}(0,1)) & \le & \liminf_{N \to \infty} \#I_N (16r_N)^4\\
  &\le& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))}{N\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))} (16r_N)^4\\
  & =&  \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{64^4}{N} = 0.
 \end{eqnarray*}
 This contradicts the assumption $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{d_b}(0,1))> 0$.

\qed

nodes.name: Vertical shortcuts from the origin S_0
nodes.statement:
Let us define the set of shortcuts from the origin as
 \[
  {\mathcal S}_0 =  \left\{ \left(0,(0,0,4^{-n})


   \right)   \;:\;   n \in a^{-1}(\{1\})  \right\},

nodes.statement:

 \[

  \right\}
 \]

 \[

 \]

nodes.name: Scale selector a via primes
nodes.statement:
Since we want to avoid self-similarity, we define the function $a$ so that every word written in the alphabets $\{0,1\}$
 appears consecutively in the sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ only some limited number of times.
 This is achieved for example by defining
 \[
  a(i) := \begin{cases}
          1, & \text{if there exists }k \text{ odd and }l \in \mathbb N\text{ such that }i = (k\ell\prod_{h < \ell}p_h+1)p_\ell\\
          0, & \text{otherwise},
         \end{cases}
 \]
 where $p_\ell$ is the $\ell$:th prime number.
nodes.statement_short: a(i)=1 iff i = (k l prod_{h<l} p_h + 1) p_l for some odd k and l; ensures no word repeats periodically.

nodes.name: No periodic repetition in the sequence a
nodes.statement: Let $\ell \geq 1$. There exists some $m \geq 1$ so that for any $i \geq 1$, there exists some $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.
nodes.label: lma:norepeat

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let us write \[ P_\ell = \left\{(k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\right\}. \] We claim that $\{P_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb N}$ is a disjointed collection of sets. In order to see this take $0 < \ell < \ell'< \infty$ and notice that on one hand for every $k \in \mathbb N$ we have $p_\ell \mid (k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell$. On the other hand, since $p_\ell \mid \prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}$, we have $p_\ell \nmid (k\ell'\prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}+1)p_{\ell'}$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Now let $\ell \geq 1$ be given. Define $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_{h}$. Then $P_\ell = \{p_\ell + m\ell k \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}$. Let $i \ge 1$ and select $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $j \equiv p_\ell \pmod{m\ell}$. Then by definition, $j \in P_\ell$. By the fact that the sets $P_{\ell'}$ are pairwise disjoint we have from the definition of $a$ that \[ a(m\ell k + p_{\ell}) = \begin{cases} 1,& \text{if }k \text{ is odd},\\ 0,& \text{if }k \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \] Thus $a(j) \neq a(j + \ell m)$.
nodes.statement_short: The sets P_l are disjoint arithmetic progressions; a alternates along P_l, so a(j) != a(j+ml) for j in P_l.

nodes.name: Claim: the sets P_l are pairwise disjoint
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.6
nodes.statement: Assume to the contrary that there exists a sequence $(\lambda_j)_{j \in \mathbb N}$, with $\lambda_j \to 0$ such that the distances $$(p,q)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d_1(\delta_{\lambda_j} (p),\delta_{\lambda_j} (q)) $$ converge pointwise to some $\rho$, and the distance $\rho$ is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. Let us now find a contradiction by using the assumed self-similarity. For this purpose let us first take a point $(0,0,s^2) \in \mathbb H$ appearing as limit of points to which there is a shortcut from the origin. In other words, take \begin{equation} s \in [1,2^4] \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty\overline{\bigcup_{i \geq j} \{\lambda_i^{-1}2^{-4(k+1)}\,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}}. \end{equation} Then we indeed have \[ \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda_j^2s^2)) = \frac12d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)), \] since $a(4(k+1))= 1$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Let us then use the function $f$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} to show that there exists $\ell \in \mathbb N$ such that $\lambda = 2^\ell$. Supposing this is not the case, we have $\lambda = t2^\ell$ for some $t \in (1,2)$ and $\ell \in \mathbb N$. By \eqref{14598015} $s$ is of the form $s=\lim_{m\to \infty} \lambda_{i_m}^{-1} 2^{-4(k_m+1)}$, with $i_m, k_m\to \infty$. Then, by the continuity of the function $f$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,\lambda^2s^2)) & = &\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &\lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} d_1(0,(0,0, t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2 4^\ell 4^{-4(k_m+1)}\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2)) \\ & \ge& \lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} f\left(t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2\right ) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ &=& f(t^2)\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &f(t^2)\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) > \frac12\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lambda \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) , \end{eqnarray*} contradicting the fact that $\rho$ is self-similar with the dilation $\lambda$. Therefore $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. Now we employ the properties of the function $a$. Let $m \in \mathbb N$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}. Since $\rho$ is self-similar with factor $2^\ell$, it is self-similar also with factor $2^{\ell m}$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformupperbound}, we have that there exists some $\eta$ such that $(1+\eta)^N = 4$ for some $N \in \mathbb N$ and if $a(n) = 1$, then \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})) \leq 0.51 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})), \qquad \forall t \in (-\eta,\eta). \end{equation} Take $j_0 \in \mathbb N$ such that for all $j \ge j_0$ we have \begin{equation} \frac{\rho(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^ks^2))}{\lambda_j^{-1} d_1(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k\lambda_j^2s^2))} \in \left(1 - \frac{1}{100}, 1 + \frac{1}{100} \right), \end{equation} for all $(i,k) \in \{0,1,\dots,2 m\ell\} \times \{0,\dots,N-1\}$. Let $n \in \mathbb Z$ be such that $(\lambda_j s)^2 \in \left[ \frac{1}{2} 4^{-n}, 2 \cdot 4^{-n}\right)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}, we have that there exists some $i \in \{0,\dots,m \ell\}$ such that $a(n+i) \neq a(n+ i + m\ell)$. We may suppose without loss of generality that $a(n+i) = 1$ so $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$. We have that there exists some $k \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ such that $4^i(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in ((1-\eta) 4^{n+i},(1+\eta) 4^{n+i})$. Thus, because $a(n+i) = 1$, we have that \begin{equation} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \overset{\eqref{e:upperbound} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\leq} 0.52 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{equation} On the other hand, because $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$ and $$4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in \left( \frac{1}{2} 4^{n+i+m\ell}, 2 \cdot 4^{n+i+m\ell} \right),$$ we have that \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) &\overset{\eqref{e:sqrt3-lower} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\geq} &\frac{99}{100} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \\ &\geq& 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k s^2)), \\ &=& 0.55 \cdot 2^{m\ell} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} Then by the self-similarity of $\rho$ with ratio $2^{m\ell}$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) & = & 2^{-m\ell}\rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2))\\ & \ge & 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts \eqref{eq:finalcontra}.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: Lemma 6.3 forces the dilation factor to be a power of 2; then Lemmas 6.1, 6.4, 6.5 compare scales with and without shortcuts.

nodes.name: Assume a self-similar blow-up rho
nodes.statement:
Assume to the contrary that there exists a sequence $(\lambda_j)_{j \in \mathbb N}$, with $\lambda_j \to 0$ such that the distances
$$(p,q)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d_1(\delta_{\lambda_j} (p),\delta_{\lambda_j} (q)) $$
converge pointwise to some $\rho$, and the distance $\rho$ is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a self-similar blow-up rho

nodes.name: Limit point (0,0,s^2) of shortcut endpoints
nodes.statement:
Let us now find a contradiction by using the assumed self-similarity.
 For this purpose let us first take a point $(0,0,s^2) \in \mathbb H$ appearing as limit of points to which there is a shortcut from the origin.
 In other words, take
 \begin{equation} s \in [1,2^4] \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty\overline{\bigcup_{i \geq j} \{\lambda_i^{-1}2^{-4(k+1)}\,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}}.
 \end{equation}
 Then we indeed have
 \[
  \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda_j^2s^2)) = \frac12d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)),
 \]
 since $a(4(k+1))= 1$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.statement_short: Limit point (0,0,s^2) of shortcut endpoints

nodes.name: Lemma 6.3 forces lambda = 2^l
nodes.statement:
Let us then use the function $f$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1}
 to show that there exists $\ell \in \mathbb N$ such that $\lambda  = 2^\ell$.
 Supposing this is not the case, we have $\lambda = t2^\ell$ for some $t \in (1,2)$ and $\ell \in \mathbb N$.
 By \eqref{14598015} $s$ is of the form $s=\lim_{m\to \infty} \lambda_{i_m}^{-1} 2^{-4(k_m+1)}$, with $i_m, k_m\to \infty$.
 Then, by the continuity of the function $f$ we have
 \begin{eqnarray*}
  \rho(0,(0,0,\lambda^2s^2)) & = &\lim_{j  \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\
& = &\lim_{m  \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} 
d_1(0,(0,0,  t^2 
\left(  \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2  
 4^\ell  4^{-4(k_m+1)}\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))
\\
  & \ge& 
  \lim_{m  \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} 
 f\left(t^2   \left(  \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2\right ) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\
&=&  f(t^2)\lim_{j  \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\
  & = &f(t^2)\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) > \frac12\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lambda \rho(0,(0,0,s^2))
  ,
 \end{eqnarray*}
 contradicting the fact that $\rho$ is self-similar with the dilation $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.3 forces lambda = 2^l

nodes.name: Self-similar with factor 2^{lm}
nodes.statement:
Therefore $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. Now we employ the properties of the function $a$.
 Let $m \in \mathbb N$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}. Since $\rho$ is self-similar with factor $2^\ell$,
 it is self-similar also with factor $2^{\ell m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Self-similar with factor 2^{lm}

nodes.name: Dyadic centres D_n
nodes.statement: Let $D_n$ denote the centers of the dyadic cubes in $\mathbb R^2$ of sidelength $2^{-n}$.

nodes.name: Level n shortcuts for d_2
nodes.statement:
Define the level $n$ shortcuts as the symmetrization of
\[
 \tilde{\mathcal S}_n = \{((x,y,z),(x,y,z)q) : (x,y) \in D_n, z \in \mathbb R, q = (0,0,\pm 4^{-n})\}.
\]

nodes.name: Shortcuts for d_2
nodes.statement:
We then construct the set of shortcuts as
\[
  \tilde{\mathcal S} = \bigcup_{n \in a^{-1}(\{1\})} \tilde{\mathcal S}_n.
\]

nodes.name: Cost function for d_2
nodes.statement:
As in the construction of $d_1$, the cost function $\tilde c : \mathbb{H} \times \mathbb{H} \to [0,\infty)$
for $(p,q) \in \tilde{\mathcal S}$ is 
\[
  \tilde c(p,q) = \frac{1}{2} d_{cc}(p,q).
\]

nodes.name: Distance d_2
nodes.statement: The distance $d_2$ is then obtained as the distance $d$ in \eqref{eq:ddef}, but now with using $\tilde c$.

nodes.name: Comparison d_cc/2 <= d_1 <= d_2 <= d_cc
nodes.statement:
Since $\tilde{\mathcal S} \subset {\mathcal S}$ and thus $\tilde c \ge c$, we have
\[
  \frac{1}{2} d_{cc} \leq d_1 \leq d_2 \leq d_{cc}. \]

nodes.name: Lower bound for d_2 off the grid
nodes.statement: There exists some absolute $\delta > 0$ so that if for any $n \in \mathbb N$, if $(x,y) \in B(D_n + (2^{-n-1},2^{-n-1}),\delta 2^{-n})$ and $t \in (1/2,2)$, then \[ d_2((x,y,z),(x,y,z + t4^{-n})) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \qquad \forall z \in \mathbb R. \]
nodes.label: l:off-grid

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.7
nodes.statement: Let $(a,b) \in D_n$ be so that $(x,y) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ ($\delta$ to be chosen later) and let ${\bf x} = (x_0,...,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $(x,y,z)$ to $(x,y,z + t4^{-n})$. Note that \[ d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sqrt{t 4^{-n}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n}. \] Suppose first that there is some $\pi(x_j) \notin B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$. As any non-vertical movement is not a shortcut, we have from the fact that $\pi(x_0) = \pi(x_N) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ that if we choose $\delta$ sufficiently small, then \[ c({\bf x}) \geq (1-2\delta) 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})). \] This would prove the statement of the lemma. Thus, we may suppose that the projection of ${\bf x}$ under $\pi$ does not go outside $B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$. But now the proof is reduced to that of the proof of Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-2}. Indeed, by the hypothesis of this subcase, the itinerary ${\bf x}$ cannot contain any level $n$ shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Either the itinerary leaves a horizontal neighbourhood (cost >= 2^{-n} up to constants) or it uses no level n shortcut and Lemma 6.4's argument applies.

  \[
    d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sqrt{t 4^{-n}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n}.
  \]

nodes.statement:
Suppose first that there is some $\pi(x_j) \notin B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$.  As any non-vertical movement is not a shortcut, we have from the fact that $\pi(x_0) = \pi(x_N) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ that if we choose $\delta$ sufficiently small, then
  \[
    c({\bf x}) \geq (1-2\delta) 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})).
  \]
  This would prove the statement of the lemma.  Thus, we may suppose that the projection of ${\bf x}$ under $\pi$ does not go outside $B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$.

nodes.name: Otherwise reduce to Lemma 6.4
nodes.statement: But now the proof is reduced to that of the proof of Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-2}.  Indeed, by the hypothesis of this subcase, the itinerary ${\bf x}$ cannot contain any level $n$ shortcuts.

nodes.name: Upper bound for d_2 on the grid
nodes.statement: For every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists $\eta \in (0,1/2)$ so that if $|t| < \eta$ and $a(n) = 1$, then for all $(x,y) \in B(D_n,\eta 2^{-n})$ and $z \in \mathbb R$ we have \[ d_2((x,y,z),(x,y,z + (1+t)4^{-n})) \leq \left( \frac{1}{2} + \epsilon \right) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})). \]
nodes.label: l:grid-upper

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.8
nodes.statement: This follows by essentially the same proof as Lemma \ref{lma:uniformupperbound}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the proof of Lemma 6.5.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.5 (distance d_2 and conclusion)
nodes.statement:
Since the shortcuts are horizontally located on the centers of the dyadic cubes, we have from an easy argument using Lemmas \ref{l:off-grid} and \ref{l:grid-upper} that no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant.

In order to see that no blow-up of $d_2$ is self-similar we argue similarly as for the distance $d_1$.
First suppose that a blow-up is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$.
This time, instead of finding a limit point $(0,0,s^2)$ of shortcuts from the origin, we find by compactness a pair of points
$(x,y,z)$, $(x,y,z + s^2)$ in $B_{d_{cc}}(0,2^5)$ with $s \in [1,2^4]$
appearing as the limit of endpoints of a sequence of shortcuts. This is possible after passing to a subsequence
because $a(4(n+1)) = 1$ for all $n$.  Observe that Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1}
holds also for $d_2$ since $d_2 \ge d_1$. As in the case of $d_1$, it then follows
via Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} that $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$.
A contradiction with self-similarity then follows again by the properties of the function $a$.
This concludes the proof of 
Theorem \ref{thm:fail}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 rule out left-invariant blow-ups of d_2; self-similarity is excluded as for d_1 via Lemma 6.3 and the function a.
